videos.transcript: Hello 大家好 欢迎收听《硅谷101》 我是泓君 过去三年 我们经历了 大模型工程能力三次概念上的进化 大家还记得 在2023年 模型刚刚出来的时候 我们都在聊 prompt engineering（提示词工程） 核心是怎么样写好一个提示词 让模型给出更好的答案 后来在2024年的时候 焦点就变成了 context engineering（上下文工程） 泡泡玛特这家公司最近怎么了 第二部分段永平对泡泡玛特 这家公司的认知是如何变化的 第三部分 段永平是如何通过卖put挣钱的 首先第一部分 先跟大家快速的理清 泡泡玛特究竟怎么了 先说市场为什么在卖 泡泡玛特的2025年年报一发布 直接交出了王炸业绩 营收371.2亿元 同比增长了184.7% 净利润130亿元 同比暴涨了284.5% 放在任何行业都是顶级的增长数据 但是诡异的是 年报发布当天 股价直接暴跌22.5% 两天累计跌了30% 市值蒸发了600亿港元 市场的恐慌主要来源于两个担心 第一就是单IP依赖的风险 泡泡玛特当前的核心是拉布布 单IP年收入占比接近四成 市场的担心就是 一个IP撑不起长期增长 万一没有后续的爆款IP 增长就会乏力 第二就是增长放缓的焦虑 泡泡玛特的CEO王宁在年报里明确说 2026年公司的增长目标是不低于20% 对比2025年180%的爆发式增速 市场直接解读为增速见顶 觉得这家公司的黄金增长期 已经过去了 所以很多投资者选择用脚投票 直接把股价砸到了160港元附近 就在市场恐慌抛售的时候 4月9号 段永平在雪球发言 "我的泡泡玛特保险公司开张了" 熟悉段永平的朋友都知道 他这句话意味着什么 段永平选择卖put的方式 开始准备建仓泡泡玛特了 但是从先前段永平的发言记录来看 他之前评价泡泡玛特是"看不懂" 为什么他现在又突然看懂了 期间到底发生了什么 接下来我们就进入第二部分 段永平对于泡泡玛特的认知变化之路 结合段永平在雪球上的发言 我把他对这家公司的认知变化 概括为三个阶段 第一阶段就是2026(口误)年之前 段永平早期明确表示 无法理解人们为什么需要盲盒 他不理解的原因在于 盲盒背后的情绪消费到底是一时潮流 还是永续需求 他当时觉得 年轻人买盲盒就是跟风炒作 就像曾经的集卡网红玩具一样 热度褪去 需求就会消失 而且他认为 泡泡玛特的生意太依赖年轻人的审美 审美变化太快 风险太高 所以他坚守不懂不做的原则 明确表示自己不会投资 但是在2026年3月 他的认知迎来了变化 3月30号 段永平表示 他收回先前 关于不投资泡泡玛特的言论 让段永平态度动摇的 我根据段永平的发言记录 揣测归纳出了三点原因 首先就是年报数据的硬实力 2025年的业绩暴涨 它不是偶然 而是持续增长的体现 因为这家公司高毛利高现金流低负债 泡泡玛特的毛利率高达72.1% 净利润35.2% 这个水平堪比茅台 卖100块钱的产品 就能产生35块的净利润 而且 这家公司还不需要大量重资产投入 生产可以外包 核心成本是设计和IP授权 回款速度快 2025年的经营现金流达到了108.65亿元 资产负债率不到30% 财务状况极其稳健 这种轻资产高盈利的模式 抗风险能力极强 大概率是段永平最看重的稳 第二就是实地考察真实需求 在欧洲的门店里 守住情绪消费的基本盘 这款茅台的社交属性苹果的体验生态 理论上 都是能够穿越周期的核心竞争力 目前 泡泡玛特的业务覆盖了20多个国家 海外收入占比达到了43.8% 但对比乐高迪士尼的全球渗透率 它的海外布局才刚刚起步 长期增长空间巨大 第三就是王宁的长期主义 他看了王宁的访谈 看到王宁主动降低增速目标 专注IP孵化 不贪短期快钱不盲目扩张的“本分” 这种企业家的特质 和段永平自己的投资哲学高度契合 让他觉得这家公司的创始人是“对的人” 第三个阶段 就是今年4月的重仓布局阶段 一般价值投资者认为 好公司好团队好价值三者缺一不可 好公司和好团队 我在上一部分已经介绍完了 最重要的就是好价格 股价暴跌之后 这家公司的估值 从40倍PE砸到了14倍左右 这里要重点说一句 估值下降的本质 是市场对于未来增长的重新定价 重点不是14倍的PE是不是便宜 而是这个估值 能不能够匹配它未来的增长质量 和确定性 如果泡泡玛特能够实现20%的增长 那么14倍的估值并不算贵 如果他守不住20%的增速 那么当前14倍的估值就算不上是便宜 从段永平的买入操作 我们可以合理推断 他认为 这家公司长期增长的确定性足够 14倍PE算得上 是已经具备安全边际的便宜价格 更关键的是 段永平看到了 市场恐惧和公司价值之间的差距 这就是价值投资的核心 别人恐惧我贪婪 聊完了段永平认知变化的过程 接下来我们再看他的操作 videos.transcript: OK. Today I turned 40. Yeah, the day I'm recording this video is my lunar birthday. And on my 40th birthday, I made a decision. I'm going to stop hustling so hard. Now, I know that might sound like I've made enough money, and I'm ready to lie flat. Actually, it's the exact opposite. It's one of the hardest things I've ever done in my life. Most people get relaxation completely wrong. Relaxing isn't lying flat, it's not just having fun, and it's definitely not a reward you only earn after you succeed. Instead, it's the prerequisite for breaking through your bottlenecks and opening the next door. And the reason I'm making it my life's focus at 40 comes down to three things: a point of confusion, a scar on my wrist, and a book. What's your name? Ray. Ray, I'm Ray. Thank you, thanks. So that confusion came from a quote by Naval. He said, if you want to get rich, spend your time learning, earning, or relaxing, outsource or ignore everything else. Learning and earning, I get that. I've been doing those two things for the last decade, and it's what I always preach on this channel and in my community. But why spend time relaxing? I could never really wrap my head around it systematically. Then, earlier this year, I randomly read a really old book called Psycho-Cybernetics, translated as Xin Li Kong Zhi Shu. After reading it, it cleared up my confusion about Naval's philosophy on relaxing. So today, I want to use my own experiences to talk about why, if we want to unlock life's next chapter, every one of us needs to learn how to relax. I'll just have a hot mocha, easy to sip. You guys always see me wearing this Apple Watch in my videos. Honestly, I don't really like wearing watches. I wear it mostly to cover up a massive scar on my left wrist. Hey, don't overthink it, I didn't cut myself or anything. But this scar, in a way, is a microcosm of my tense, wound-up life. This is my birthday dinner. When I was a freshman in high school, my mom opened a small restaurant outside the coal mine where we lived. It was a tiny business, but grueling work. Whenever I went home for the weekend, I'd go help out, often working late into the night, and then we'd push our tricycle back home. One day, I think the gas tank ran out or something, I forget the exact details. I just remember it was just me and my mom, and a bunch of customers were waiting, getting super impatient. So I took a kitchen knife to chop some wood and help start a fire. But I accidentally hacked right into my left wrist. Blood just started spraying everywhere. I could literally see the bone. I was terrified. But I didn't dare tell my mom, afraid I'd interrupt her work. I just told her I cut my hand by accident, grabbed my wrist, and ran to a small clinic. The doctor there stopped the bleeding and gave me a bunch of stitches. The clinic was super sketchy, and the doctor's skills were pretty limited. So when the wound healed, the nerves were messed up. To this day, the area around my thumb is totally numb. I can't feel a thing there, but if you touch the scar, it hurts like crazy and gets super tingly. So if anyone ever gets into a fight with me, all they have to do is hit my left wrist hard, and they can take me down instantly. When I got back to school with this injury and people asked what happened, I started lying. I said I was playing around with a kitchen knife and accidentally slashed myself while hacking at stuff. And this lie had a few different versions. Like sometimes, depending on who I was talking to, I'd say I got slashed in a fight when I was a kid. It made me sound tough. I told these lies so many times that eventually, I kind of believed them myself. It became my default answer whenever anyone asked. I didn't even realize I was lying anymore. So why did I lie? Originally, it was just because I didn't want people looking down on me. Other kids went on vacations during their time off, while I spent my holidays working for survival, helping out in a tiny, run-down restaurant, and hacking myself in a moment of panic. Later on, I just wanted to hide the scar and everything it represented deep down inside, to give myself a goal and the strength to change my destiny against all odds. So I just kept holding my breath, pushing through, trying to force my fate to change through sheer hustle. My sophomore year of high school, I worked insanely hard. I studied until 1 or 2 AM every night and woke up at 5. I shot up to third place in my science track, and kept my grades top-tier all the way through senior year. Everyone thought I was going to a top university. But I bombed the entrance exam and only got into a second-tier college. But then a magical thing happened when I went to this second-tier college. Without the pressure of the gaokao, without everyone's expectations and eyes on me, I actually started to let loose and be myself. I started reading, listening to English podcasts, even working part-time and starting mini-businesses. That period was the fastest time of growth and transformation in my entire life. In a way, it made me who I am today. OK, OK, I gotta stop here, or I could talk about myself all day. So why am I telling you all this? What does it have to do with relaxing? Well, after reading Psycho-Cybernetics, and looking back at this and many similar experiences in my life, I noticed a pattern with myself. Whenever I'm tense and wound up, I usually mess things up. To use a trendy phrase, the harder I try, the worse I fail. And it's only when I relax that good things actually happen. I've been saying this phrase a lot lately. It's "Good things only happen when you are relaxed." Why is that? In the book, the author talks about a success mechanism. In English, it's called the success mechanism. He says that built into every one of our subconscious minds is an auto-navigation system, just like a missile's guidance system. It automatically corrects your course and guides you toward your target. You don't need to tell it how to take every single step. You just set the target and let it run. It's basically what we mean when we say "manifesting your desires." There's a quote in The Alchemist that goes, "When you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it." I'm sure most people have had experiences like this. But here's the catch: this system has one condition to operate. You have to be relaxed enough. When you're tense, anxious, and desperately trying to micromanage every single step, your conscious mind forces its way in and tries to hijack the auto-pilot. And the result is, you just jam the whole system up. It's like walking while carrying a full glass of water, trying not to spill it. The more you think, "Don't spill," and the harder you stare at the glass, the more you end up spilling. But if you ignore it, stop caring, and just relax, the water stays right in the cup. The book refers to this as the creative mechanism. It gets locked down by your forebrain. So the more you want it, the worse you perform. Specifically, your inability to relax holds you back in these four dimensions. We often think that pressure comes from motivation. I pushed myself to study hard to crush the gaokao, driven by this core belief. Counterintuitively though, that understanding might be completely wrong. The book mentions an experiment: when animals learn about a new environment without too much pressure, they form a very broad cognitive map, exploring all sorts of possibilities and gaining a comprehensive understanding of their surroundings. But if the pressure is super high, that cognitive map shrinks drastically. They only focus on the most urgent thing right in front of them, and go completely blind to everything else. "Pressure retards learning." Pressure directly slows down your learning. And it doesn't just make you slow; it makes your learning narrow. The higher the pressure, the more inefficient and narrow your learning becomes. This makes you inflexible. When you're finally facing a real challenge, your performance naturally drops. That explains why I messed up my college entrance exam. Because I didn't just fail from being too nervous and jamming my success mechanism. Fundamentally, learning under all that pressure made my scope way too narrow. I only knew how to take tests, and only specific kinds of tests. My whole way of thinking was completely rigid. So when faced with a real challenge like the Gaokao, I had zero flexibility and no ability to adapt. Looking at the bigger picture, this also explains a phenomenon a lot of people feel but can't quite put into words. Why is it that "small-town test machines" like me, who didn't come from a great background, did well in school and were great at taking tests, but once we enter society, we end up performing worse than kids who grew up in more relaxed environments, even if their grades weren't as good? We used to think it was just because they had more resources or better connections. But this book made me realize there's a deeper reason: we thought we were learning better, but actually, we were learning much narrower. They grew up in a more relaxed environment, so their cognitive map is way broader than ours. Meanwhile, those small-town test machines are much more likely to face high-pressure situations. So at the end of the day, "happy learning" actually makes sense. And our high-pressure background has been affecting our entire life trajectory. Now, this isn't to say that studying and working hard under massive pressure can't bring you success. But the secret is, if you want to unlock even greater success, you need to give yourself room to breathe and learn how to relax. I know what you're gonna say: "Easy for you to say! You can't just relax on command." "What if my circumstances don't allow me to relax?" "Rui, when you were a small-town test machine, you couldn't relax either, right?" "Now that you're well-off, it's easy for you to preach." Yeah, I don't deny that. For a lot of people in crisis mode, it's impossible to completely let go. But we have to understand that "relaxing" is actually a spectrum, not just a single state. And that brings me to my second point: your inability to relax is an overreaction. It turns you into a reactor in life, rather than an actor. The book says humans are fundamentally actors, not reactors. We aren't just ships drifting in the wind. We have goals and we have direction. If your reaction to your environment isn't pushing your goals forward, or is even holding you back, what you really should do is just not react. The worrying, the anxiety, and the stressing we do every day—that's exactly this kind of useless reaction. They don't help you move forward; they only keep you stuck. What you really need to do is stop reacting. For example, the book points out that the reason most of us worry, get anxious, and panic essentially stems from a really terrible mental habit: you always feel like you should be doing a million things right now. While you're working on Thing A, you suddenly remember Thing B isn't done, you want to do Thing C, and Thing D can't be delayed either. And the next passage from the author is something I absolutely love. He says that even on your busiest day, every single task can only come to you one by one. It has to. No matter how many problems, tasks, or pressures you have, they can only line up single file and come at you one at a time. That's just an objective law of reality. So when you have a million things swirling in your head, you're actually violating that reality. Because we overreact, we end up procrastinating, avoiding things, overthinking, worrying, or even getting crushed by the pressure. We fail to act as the one in control, deciding what to focus on in this exact moment, and that leads to us doing a terrible job at everything. That's why so many productivity books emphasize single-tasking and push back against multitasking. And when books teach us mindfulness and focusing on the present, they're essentially just following this exact same rule of taking things one step at a time. They're telling us to relax and stop overreacting. It's just that they usually focus more on the spiritual or wellness side without really explaining the underlying mechanics. But this book figured it all out and explained the logic perfectly over half a century ago. And this applies not just to a specific task, but to our entire life journey. We always say "life is a journey," but honestly, a lot of times we don't really grasp what that actually means. In recent years, a lot of books have been preaching "enjoy the process" and downplaying the importance of goals. Early this year on our channel, we read a book called Tiny Experiments, which even goes as far as saying you shouldn't set goals at all, you should set experiments. But that totally contradicts another popular narrative. There are endless "success" books and productivity guides teaching you how to set goals, make plans, and break down execution. So which one is actually right? Well, Psycho-Cybernetics gives a crystal clear answer: they're both right, you've just messed up the ratio. The book says humans are naturally goal-oriented animals. Without a goal, you wouldn't even start. So how could there even be a process? Therefore, goals are absolutely necessary. But once you've set that goal, you should actually be in "journey mode" for the vast majority of the time. In journey mode, you are an actor. You decide exactly where to step, and you even get to decide to enjoy the scenery along the way. But when you're only staring at the goal, you end up overreacting. Trying too hard turns you into a reactor, and you end up losing your footing. What you really should do is spend most of your time watching the road right under your feet, and only occasionally look up to make sure you're still heading the right way. Yet so many of us do the exact opposite. We spend too little time in journey mode and stare way too hard at the goal. The more you stare, the more the pressure pushes you from being an actor to a reactor, and you end up moving slower by trying to rush. The heavier your goals are, the more you need to learn how to relax. This is incredibly relevant to my life right now. I've mentioned before that I've achieved relative financial and time freedom, and now I only work on things I love, aiming for big goals. But I found that with such massive goals and so many projects, I'm constantly trying to solve every single problem in front of me as quickly as possible. It leaves me feeling suffocated. Sometimes I get so overwhelmed by the tasks— wanting to do everything right now but ending up doing nothing at all— that I forget to focus on the process and even want to just give up. And worse, it makes me beat myself up, thinking I'm just not capable enough. And that brings us to the next major way pressure ruins our progress. My 40th birthday is over. Let's go to the studio. Let's see if that security cat is still there. The other day on Twitter, I saw a highly debated clip of the billionaire Marc Andreessen. It sparked a ton of controversy. In an interview, he said he rarely self-reflects. He's even read over 400 biographies of great entrepreneurs, and found that almost none of them engage in self-reflection. "You don't have any levels of introspection." "Yes, zero. As little as possible." "Why?" "Move forward. Go. Yeah, I, I don't know." "I just find people who dwell on the past get stuck in the past. It's, it's just, it's a real problem and it's a, it's a problem at work and it's a problem at home." He criticized self-reflection as a modern invention, a psychological and philosophical movement driven by guilt. Great figures of the past didn't do this. They only looked outward and forward to build great things, instead of sitting around criticizing themselves and doubting themselves while living in the past. As soon as he said that, the internet blew up. His critics and his supporters started arguing fiercely, and Marc himself didn't let it go either— he kept getting into endless debates with his haters right there on Twitter. Now, I know his statement is definitely extreme, but after I watched it, I thought, doesn't this perfectly align with the point I've been trying to make? If we apply this idea of "self-reflection" to the success mechanism we've been talking about today, it's basically an error-correction mechanism. There's nothing inherently wrong with correcting errors. Your success mechanism needs it, just like a missile has to constantly adjust its trajectory to hit the target. But the book immediately follows up with a crucial prerequisite: for this error correction to actually work, it has to be subconscious, automatic and spontaneous. Meaning, the correction has to happen at a subconscious level. It has to be automatic and unprompted. Any conscious effort to engage in self-criticism and self- correction is fundamentally over-correcting, and it does more harm than good. Why? For example, if you're giving a speech on stage, your eyes will naturally scan the audience's faces. And if someone frowns, you might subconsciously slow down your pace, or explain things in a different way. You won't even realize you're doing it. That's course correction at the subconscious level. It runs quietly in the background, highly accurate, and very efficient. But if, during your speech, someone suddenly stands up and boos you, or the voice of self-criticism in your head gets loud enough, then this correction signal gets dragged from the subconscious right into your conscious mind. Your focus is completely shattered. You start doubting and second-guessing yourself, your system overloads, and you panic. The exact same signal helps you when it's subconscious, but becomes pure interference when it hits the conscious level. That's exactly how self-criticism works. Of course you need to correct mistakes and improve, but you should let your subconscious handle that process— auto-correcting and auto-adjusting. When you drag it into your conscious mind, turning it into "Why am I so bad?" or "I messed up again," or "Am I just a failure?"—then you're no longer correcting, you're attacking yourself. Your success mechanism isn't being fixed, it's being suppressed. So when we talk about relaxing, it really just means letting your conscious mind step back and letting your subconscious take the wheel. Being tense is just your conscious mind fighting for control. When your success mechanism is suppressed, the most obvious symptom is that you're afraid to be yourself. Why emphasize "being yourself"? Because deep down, every single one of us has a true self, and a natural instinct to express it. True success is finding and unleashing that authentic version of you, and answering that ultimate question: "Who am I?" But excessive self-criticism actively crushes that expression. I often say that as a YouTuber, succeeding is actually really simple: you just need to take how you express yourself off-camera and bring that exact same energy on-camera. Off-camera, when nobody's around, you can make goofy faces in the mirror, sing freely, crack jokes, totally full of confidence. But the second the camera rolls, you become a totally different person. You can tangibly feel yourself holding back. But notice that most of the time, what's suppressing you isn't the audience, it's you. It's your own conscious mind. When you drop that self-consciousness and hit a state of flow, that's when you achieve your maximum self-expression, and that is your ultimate potential. And this state of flow is the deepest form of relaxation. Very few people can actually pull it off, myself included. But for those who can, it's almost impossible for them not to succeed. Now, the stage or camera example is specific, but it's also universal, because we're all performing on the stage of our own lives. A lot of the time, we don't even realize we're suppressing ourselves. And the more you suppress yourself, refusing to release your unique personality and nature, the further away you get from the success you want. That's why, at 40 years old, I decided to pursue just being "loose," to capture that feeling of true relaxation. I get the logic, but so often I still can't help it. I still tense up and consciously criticize myself. So that leads to what I want to share next—the most important lesson I learned from Psycho-Cybernetics: and that is saying goodbye to the straw man from your past. Going back to that Marc Andreessen interview, did you notice? He said self-criticism is a guilt-driven psychological philosophy, and people trapped in it usually live in the past. Well, this book mentions the exact same thing. The author says, "Don't fight the straw man out of the past." Stop wrestling with the ghost of yesterday. A lot of the tension and self-criticism you feel right now isn't reflecting anything happening in the present; it's reacting to a threat that hasn't existed for years. It's like how the college entrance exams are long gone, but so many of us still dream about them, and most of the time, it's a nightmare. I often talk with my friends about how so many people have been stuck in survival mode for so long. Always the reactor, always on edge. But you're not in that environment anymore. You are safe now. Yet your system is still running on that old code. We don't know how to play in exploration mode. We don't know how to go back to being an actor, because we've been tense for so long we think it's the only way to live. And that scar I mentioned at the start of this video? That's my straw man. I used lies to bury it in the deepest corner. And by avoiding it, I couldn't ever say goodbye to it. It pops up from time to time to stop you from being your true self. So I'm putting it out there today, because I finally want to say goodbye to it. Your straw man might look different from mine. It might be that one time you were rejected as a kid, or a moment of public humiliation, or the fear you internalized after being punished, or the constant hint that you just weren't good enough. But whatever it is, it belongs to the past. It has no place in your present. In The Courage to Be Disliked, which we read before, there's a concept a lot of people struggle to accept: that trauma doesn't exist. It doesn't mean pain isn't real. It means your current reaction isn't being forced on you by that past event. You have a choice. This is exactly what Psycho-Cybernetics is saying too. The book makes it very clear: when faced with a fake problem, the best reaction is actually no reaction. Reacting makes you a reactor—it makes you tense. Not reacting makes you the actor—it makes you relaxed. So when we talk about learning to relax, it essentially means learning not to react to non-existent problems, to problems we've blown completely out of proportion, to emotions and environments that can hurt us. Not reacting. Capturing that relaxation, letting the straw man fall, letting your success mechanism genuinely run for you again, achieving maximum self-expression, and unlocking the next chapter of your life. This is why, at 40, I decided to stop pushing so hard, and made learning to relax a major life priority. Naval says there are three things in life: learn, earn, relax. I've spent the last 30 years doing the first two, and now it's time to start the third. Because "Good things only happen when you are relaxed."

AI的文章就是一个例子，明天盘后大科技又要集中发布财报，同一天还有美联储的利率决议，这种超级密集的窗口，本来就是机构借题发挥的时候。 财报只要有一点点不够完美，或者管理层措辞稍微保守，机构都可能先卖再说。那今天可以拿open AI的内部数字砸盘，明天就可以拿大科技财报砸盘。总之，市场永远不缺砸盘的理由，但我们一定要理智地认识到，这些都只是短期的杂音。 真正的问题不是有没有砸盘理由，而是这些理由能不能改变。AI的主线在我看来是不能的，波动不是趋势，反转，更多是机构借题发挥，借机换手。所以这期节目我不会跟大家纠结某一天盘前盘后的涨跌，我只讲两个决定，中期方向的核心问题。 第一就是为什么估值比大家以为的要便宜很多，而且盈利还在持续超预期。第二，为什么AI资本开支这个之前市场最担心的问题正在从风险故事逐渐变成变现故事？那我们先讲第一条，估值没有大家想的贵，盈利增速比大家预期的也要快。 把这两件事放在一起，我们才能够真正理解这轮行情为什么才刚刚开始。最近很多人看到指数创新高，就本能地说一句太贵了。可问题是今天的大科技真的有大家嘴里说的那么贵吗？著名的阿波罗资管的首席经济学家在上周发布了一张图，是我觉得最近最有杀伤力的。 一张图，他不只看了标普五百整体的估值，还看了标普五百信息技术板块前十大公司的估值，分别是英伟达苹果微软博通甲骨文镁光AMD思科等等。通过看这些股票的加权前瞻市盈率，也就是按照未来12个月的每股收益来计算的。 市盈率结论非常反直觉。数据显示，这批最核心的科技巨头在2024年最热的时候前瞻市盈率接近四十倍，但到现在已经押回到了二十倍左右。当然，在经历了上周的反弹以后，这些估值有小幅的增加，但也依然远低于2024年的峰值。 所以我们可以看到这些公司的估值已经回到了AI热潮初期的水平。因此我们可以非常直观地看到，现在整体大科技股的估值绝对没有到特别贵的地步，甚至是相对便宜的未知。而且这件事最重要的地方不是估值跌了，而是这些股票明明涨了很多了。 估值为什么反而回落了呢？这是因为它们的盈利长得更快，价格在涨，但分母涨得更快，所以估值就被稀释掉了。那泡沫顶部通常是什么画面？是股价继续涨，估值继续扩，但盈利却开始跟不上。可今天我们看到的不是这个画面，而是股价涨了。 盈利长得更快，结果估值反而就被压下来了。这不是泡沫顶部的特征，更像一轮主升浪的初中段。所以从估值的角度来看，现在依然是相对较低的，还有进一步扩张的可能性。如果我们把盈利的数据再放进来，这个逻辑只会更应根据facts。 最新的统计显示，标普五百指数今年第一季度的混合净利润率达到了13.4%。如果最终确认这个预期能够变成事实，那它将是faxed从2009年开始追踪这个数据以来的历史最高值。而且我们注意这并不是一次性的异常值。 上一个季度的记录是13.2，而那个记录就是在他之前那个季度刚刚创下的，已经连续多个季度再创新高。分析师对2026年全年的净利润率的预测是13.9%，而过去十年的平均水平只有11%，这也就意味着今天的企业。 每一块钱的收入能挤出来的利润比过去任何一个可比时期都要多。整个盈利能力的台阶已经被永久性地提高了一层。再看超预期的幅度，目前已经公布的第一季度财报里，84%的公司盈利超过了分析师的预期，超预期幅度平均达到了12.3%。 这两个数字在过去五年分别对应的均值是78%和7.3，这也就是说，这一季的超预期，无论是发生的比例还是幅度都是高于过去五年的均值了，所以这一系列的估值和盈利数据都指向我们没有处在很严重的泡沫，反而基本面。 有非常明显的改善迹象，甚至还在不断地加速。当然，现在大科技平均二十多倍的市盈率，当然不是特别的便宜，但也绝对不是只剩下情绪支撑的状态。他们后面站着的是订单，是积压的合同，是利润率，是现金流，是还没有体现到财报里的未来承诺金额。 那把估值和盈利这两件事放在一起，结论就变得非常清楚。今天这个市场并不是在泡沫顶部，他更像是一轮主升浪的初中段。我对年底标普五百的判断是至少八千点，也就是从当前的位置算，大概还有11%的上涨空间，这个幅度不需要估值重新从二十倍。 吹回到四十倍，只需要盈利继续增长预期继续上修。而就目前的数据来看，这两件事都在发生，而且在加速发生。所以从估值的角度来看，整体美股依然有继续走高的空间，那第二个理由也是现在市场分歧最大的地方，我们要重点讲一下。 那就是AI的变现可见度比前几个月明显提高了。之前三月份整体美股大幅回调的核心原因就是投资者认为现在AI的大幅开支最终很有可能赚不回来或者转的太慢了。但我认为现在市场对AI资本开支最强烈的那种恐惧。 正在阶段性的降温。之前市场最怕的一句话就是钱花出去了。AI到底什么时候才能把钱赚回来？那这个问题到今天的确依然没有彻底的回答完，但他已经不像前几个月前那么模糊了。最大的变化在于市场现在看到的不再只是巨头疯狂砸资本支出。 而是开始初步看到企业端的真实落地，节省下来的真实成本，以及更清晰的订单和合同和越来越强的需求可见度。那这两天有一条消息，我认为是一个里程碑的事件。就在昨天，微软宣布将Co pilot部署到知名的咨询公司埃森哲。 全球约74.3万名员工，这是迄今为止规模最大的单次企业级Co pilot部署。那埃森哲从2023年8月开始试点，从几百人的小范围测试到两万人，再到后来承诺的三十万人，到今天一次性扩展到全世界全公司74万人。 从数字上来看，这笔交易的绝对金额在大厂营收里是很小的一部分。但我认为这件事的意义远远不止是一笔订单，它代表的是一个主题的开始。全球最大的咨询公司之一，选择把AI工具全面嵌入到每一个员工的日常工作流，而不是作为可选工具。 让员工自己决定用不用那埃森哲内部的数据非常有说服力。已经使用了一段时间的二十万人员工队列里，越活越使用率达到了89%。这个数字对于任何企业软件都算极高了，更别说是一个需要额外付费的AI插件97%的员工。 表示，Co pilot帮助他们把日常重复性任务的完成速度提升了最多15倍53%，报告了显著的生产力提升。其中有一个具体案例，通过Co pilot驱动的销售分析工具，活跃使用的销售人员比未使用的同事多开发出了43%的销售机会。 这些数字都不是假设是真实的，已经跑过24万人规模的实测数据。更重要的是，这件事告诉市场的信号，当埃森哲这种全球顶级的咨询服务公司，他自己每天在帮客户做AI转型，选择把Co pilot变成全公司的标配，它传递的信号不只是我们在用。 而是这已经是可以规模化部署对生产力产生真实影响的工具了。如果他们这种在AI落地上走得最快的公司，都在今天才从三十万用户扩展到了74万，这告诉我们这个主题还在早期，未来会有越来越多的公司下类似的订单。 而这就是AI进一步大规模变现的重要信号之一。而且微软自己的数据显示，Co pilot月活用户现在是一薏仁儿Accenture这一笔就贡献了快1%，这就是我说的收入不多但主题很重要的意思，它是一个信号，一个证明AI工具已经从试用。 进入全面制度化部署的信号，而制度化部署一旦开始，就很难逆转，而且速度只会越来越快。而且不仅如此，近期有越来越多企业落地AI的证据，比如四大之一的德勤德罗，他们最新的2026年调查里显示66%。 和企业已经报告看到了生产率和效率的提升，40%的企业已经看到了成本的下降，而真正已经看到收入增长的只有20%。但我反而觉得这组数据特别健康，因为它说明AI第一阶段最真实的兑现路径本来就不是先爆发式增收。 而是先将本先省人工先省工时，先把原来需要很多人做的重复性工作自动化，所以AI帮助最先进入利润表的不一定是新收入，而是少花的钱，这才是企业AI当下最现实最可持续的起点，那这对我们打工人来说绝对是坏消息。 因为注定会有越来越多的裁员，但对企业的灵力和股价来说，绝对是一个重要的利好。另外一组数据也非常有意思，从亚特兰大联储调查近750家企业高管得到的数据来看，AI对劳动生产率的年化贡献在2025年大约是0.8个百分点。 2026年预计跳升到两个百分点以上，落到具体岗位。该调查显示，软件开发岗的生产力提升被测算为26%，新入职的客服人员效率提升达到了34%，这些数字已经开始在企业的成本报表里体现出来。 而且AI不需要100%替代掉我们现在每一个人的工作，只要能把我们的效率提升30%到五十，那这就意味着以前两个人的工作或者三个人的工作，一个人就可以做了，而这也就带来了相应比例的裁员。而且谷歌关于AI agent的研究。 进一步证明了这一点。在已经使用生成式AI的企业里，52%已经把AI agent放进了生产环境，主要集中在客服营销安全运营和技术支持这些最容易直接省钱最容易直接提效的场景。所以AIA真的来临也进一步加速了这个过程。 AI的变现落地，至少在企业端来看，路径已经变得更加清晰了。而且虽然近期市场都在批评这些云厂商资本开支实在是太高了，但我们要注意一件事，所有这些公司的管理层在最近的电话会议上都说了同一句话，就是算力是供给受限，而不是需求受限。 那他的意思就是我们想多卖，但是产能不够。所以如果大量的资本开支并不是赌未来的需求，而是变成了现在已有订单，但产能不够用，市场对它的估值框架就应该根本性的改变。对于市场来说，这个变化非常关键。AI的资本支出不再只是先把钱砸下去。 希望以后有需求，而越来越像需求合同预付款承诺已经在那里，所以现在必须扩产能。前者是一个风险故事，后者是一个能见度很高的执行故事。所以当市场开始用后者来理解AI的资本开支，那对整个AI主线的估值容忍度。 就会系统性的提升。这是我认为当前市场最被低估的一个认知转变，它还没有完全被价格反映进去，但它正在发生。所以这第二个理由简单来说就是AI不是还没开始赚钱，而是很多人还在用错误的标准看他总在等一个突然多出几百亿美元新收入的瞬间。 才愿意承认AI开始兑现。可在我们真实的世界里，AI往往先从省钱开始，先从裁掉一些岗位，少招一些人，少花一些公式开始，也就是先从费用端改善开始，然后随着部署越来越深，在慢慢长出更大的收入池。 我们今天已经能够在利润表里看到这里的第一层，第二层，也就是真正大规模的新收入。我认为还在路上，但离我们也不远了当然也正因为市场对未来两三年的变现可能性还存在很多争议，市场才会出现三月份那样的反复剧烈波动。 今天opening I这条新闻就可以被拿来砸盘。明天大科技财报一样可以先拿来卖一波。但我还是那句话，这些都只能够造成短期的震荡，但改变不了真正的方向。因为现在从基本面的角度来看，路径已经变得非常清晰。首先估值比大多数人都以为的要更加便宜。 第二就是AI的变现路径已经在变得越来越清晰，所以我认为今年年底标普五百指数至少能够涨到八千点，当然在这个过程中也会是非常坎坷的，很多杂音都会不断的给美股造成短期的震荡，那真正的大行情从来都不是在所有人。 都舒服，所有消息都完美的时候展开的。它往往就是在分期里，在波动里，在一次次是不是不行了的怀疑里，走出最有杀伤力的主绳端。所以如果今天你问我一句最简单的话，这一轮美股是不是已经涨的差不多了？我的答案依然是不是。 这轮大涨才刚刚开始。好的，以上就是本期的视频，如果您看到这里了，也一定记得给我留下一个赞，并且麻烦您在评论区留下一个手动的赞，让更多的朋友们看到这期视频。再次感谢朋友们一直以来的大力支持，我们下期节目再见。

这个法则是美国开国三杰之一 本杰明·富兰克林 (Benjamin Franklin) 的时间管理原则 作为著名的物理学家和发明家 他最早提出了电荷守恒定律 他还是美国独立战争时重要的领导人之一 也是美国首位邮政总局局长 可以说 富兰克林的人生就是许多杰出人物的生命总和 那么一个人到底怎样在一生中有限的时间里 做出那么多伟大的事的呢？ 在富兰克林的相关著作中 有人挖掘出了富兰克林成年以后 一直遵循的时间管理原则 他坚持在每个工作日 周一到周五 专门空出 1 个小时进行学习 学习的内容包含各个领域 同时他还会制定个人成长目标 并会追踪和反思自己的实践效果 这样下来一周就有 5 个小时 后来人们也将这个法则称为 富兰克林的 5 小时法则 这个原则看上去极其简单 但实际上坚持下来的难度非常高 五小时法则的核心在于 给日程留白 而不在于每天 1 小时这个量化标准 并获得观察问题的新视角 把无意义的事情剔除 给生活留白 可以让我们有时间认真考虑 自己想要学习的东西 这样才能提升自己 而不是漫无目的的做事却毫无进步 既然我们一周只抽出五小时的时间学习 那就一定要学会高效输入和输出 推崇这个法则的成功人士 往往会分成三个部分来进行 首先是阅读 埃隆 马斯克 (Elon Musk) 就说过 他是通过阅读学会了如何制造火箭 并因此创立了 SpaceX
